title: Garlic mustard in the garden
subtitle: A native biennial with garlicky leaves available from autumn through to late spring.
excerpt: Garlic mustard is a native hedgerow biennial that produces garlicky, peppery leaves from autumn to late spring. Let it self-seed in a shaded or semi-wild area and it becomes self-maintaining. Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked. It is also a foodplant for orange-tip butterfly larvae.
sourceNotes: Species information from Flora of the British Isles (Clapham, Tutin, Warburg, 1952). Edibility notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Butterfly foodplant data from Butterfly Conservation.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant that completes its life cycle in two years (rosette year, then flower and seed), but maintains a presence in the garden by setting seed freely. Unlike a true perennial, individual plants die after setting seed; the stand continues from the seedlings they leave behind. Foxglove, honesty, and garlic mustard all behave this way.

content.text: Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata) is a UK native

found in hedgerows and woodland edges. In the garden it fills shaded and semi-shaded ground and provides a winter and spring harvest of garlicky leaves. It self-seeds freely and needs no annual replanting once established in a suitable spot.

Collect seed in July from wild plants or garden plants (allow a few to flower and set seed). Sow in August to September in a shaded or semi-shaded area: under trees, along a north-facing fence, or in a hedgerow edge. Surface sow and do not cover: the seed needs light to germinate. A first-year rosette of heart-shaped leaves appears; the plant flowers in its second year.

Pick young leaves from October onwards through winter and spring. The leaves have a mild garlic-mustard flavour: sharp and green, best used in small quantities in salads or as a salsa verde ingredient. Older leaves become more bitter as the plant bolts in spring. The flowers in April and May are edible and milder than the leaves.

attrs.title: Orange-tip butterfly
attrs.body: Garlic mustard is one of the main foodplants for orange-tip butterfly larvae in the UK. The female lays eggs on the flower stems in April and May. The caterpillars eat the developing seed pods. If you find small green caterpillars on the plant in May or June, leave the plant undisturbed until the caterpillars have pupated. Cut after the caterpillars have finished feeding rather than before.
